Caṇḍeśvara
------------------------------------------
He is one of the attendant deities of शिव. According to the mythological lore he was a ब्राह्मण boy, Vicāraśarman by name, who rose to that status by his intense devotion to शिव.
Iconographically, he is shown as a fierce deity, holding weapons of war and destruction like the bow, arrow, trident, chisel, noose and so on. Though independent shrines dedicated to him are not uncommon, he is generally installed in every शिव temple in the north eastern corner, facing south. Devotees believe that he can act as a mediator interceding with the Lord on their behalf. Hence supplication before him is a duty of every devotee visiting a शिव temple.
He is also known as Caṇḍi and Caṇḍeśa.
Caṇḍeśvara (14th cent. A.D.) of मिथिला is a very important compiler of digests on धर्मशास्त्रस्. He was a minister as well as the chief justice at the court of the king Harisiṁhadeva of Tirhut (now in Bihar). He belonged to the Karṇāta family. स्मृतिरत्नाकर or Ratnā-kara is the extensive digest compiled by him. Divided into seven sections—each containing the word ‘ratnākara’ as part of the title—it deals with kṛtya (what ought to be done), दान (gifts), vyavahāra (judicial procedure), शुद्धि (purificatory rites), पूजा (ritualistic worship), vivāda (disputes—civil and criminal laws) and गृहस्थ (duties of householders). Kṛtyacintā-मणि and Rājanītiratnākara are his other works considered important.
Later writers on धर्मशास्त्रस् from मिथिला and Vaṅga (Bengal) have been greatly influenced by him.

cāṇḍāla
(‘one who wears terrible ornaments’)
------------------------------------------
From the Vedic days certain groups of people used to be kept outside the pale of civilized society. ‘Aspṛśyas’ or ‘untouchables’ was the general name given to most of them since any kind of contact or proximity with them was considered polluting. This was mostly due to their horrendous ways of living and avocations fraught with potential dangers to the general health of the society.
The cāṇḍālas—also spelt as ‘caṇḍālas’—are an important group of aspṛśyas. मनु defines the चाण्डाल as one born from a ब्राह्मण woman by a śūdra ड़थेर् (vide मनुस्मृति 10.12). Other smṛtis define the word in other ways.
The cāṇḍālas were expected to live in their own colonies outside the village or town. But they were given to roaming. Their wealth was dogs and donkeys. They lived by cleaning the dirt of the village or town. They ate the carcasses of dead animals and carried corpses of persons who had no relatives, as also looked after the च्रेमतिओन् or बुरिअल् grounds. They acted as executioners of people sentenced to death by the king. They wore ornaments of lead, iron or leather.
The cāṇḍālas were perhaps the conquered aboriginal tribes, dropouts from the society who never cared to follow its norms, abominable sinners and those following dreadful occupations.
See also ASPṚŚYATĀ.

Caṇḍī
(‘the ferocious’)
------------------------------------------
Caṇḍī is one of the names of the goddess दुर्गा. The book expounding her exploits is also called ‘Caṇḍī’. For details see DEVĪMĀHĀTMYA.

Caṇḍīpāṭha
(‘recitation of the चण्डी’)
------------------------------------------
Recitation of stotras or hymns has long been accepted as a part of the Hindu religious discipline. Its immense popularity can be gauged from the fact that the Hindu hymnal literature extant today is as vast as the sky and as deep as the ocean.
Some of these hymns like the विष्णु-sahasranāma, the दुर्गासप्तशती (also known as देवीमाहात्म्य and चण्डी) and the ललितासहस्रनाम have acquired an esoteric significance, so much so, that they are considered as ‘mantras’ or mystic formulae. Consequently, ceremonial recitals of these texts have also been prescribed, often for the fulfilment of specific desires.
The चण्डी or दुर्गासप्तशती is a basic text of the शाक्त cult or the cult of the Divine मोथेर्. Its ceremonial recital is called चण्डीपाठ. The recital can be done on any day or days, but the 8th, 9th and the 14th days of the dark lunar fortnight have been specially recommended.
Since the ceremonial recital is equi-valent to worship, many preliminary disciplines that apply to the latter, apply to the former also. For instance: आचमन (ceremonial sipping of water), प्राणायाम (regulation of breath), सङ्कल्प (religious resolve), dīpasthāpana (establishing a lighted lamp as a witness) and so on. A regular worship has to be offered to the book that is used for the recital. The recital itself should be done audibly and clearly since that is believed to create a wonderful atmosphere, in which the deity presents herself. The main text is preceded by certain hymns like the Kavaca and followed by others like the रहस्यत्रय. A regular होम or havan is to be done after the chanting is completed.
Normally one is expected to chant all the thirteen chapters—which are divided into three books called Caritras—together at one sitting. If this is not possible, alternative modes have also been recommended. Details can be learnt from standard works on the subject or from the adepts in the field.
Recitation by others—competent brāhmaṇas—may also be arranged, the benefit accruing to the person who arranges it. Recital of the चण्डी a hundred times (Śatacaṇḍī) or a thousand times (Sahasracaṇḍī) are done this way and are invariably for the good of the entire community or society or country.
The recital of the चण्डी is said to confer innumerable fruits, from the lowest secular ones to the highest spiritual enlightenment.
See also DEVĪMĀHĀTMYA.

Caṇḍīdāsa
(‘servant of चण्डी’)
------------------------------------------
Throughout the history of India, religious lyrics have proved to be immen-sely popular with the masses. They have often shaped their philosophy of life too.
During the middle ages, when the cult of कृष्ण-भक्ति was gradually gaining ground, the compositions of चण्डीदास (in the Middle Bengali language) became very popular. ‘Baḍu’ चण्डीदास, as he was best known, preceded श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A. D. 1486-1534) and is assigned to the 15th cent. A. D. He belonged to Chātna and was a member of the Vaiṣṇava Sahajīya cult. His Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtana is a remarkable poem on the कृष्ण legend in that language. It consists of a chain of lyric songs depicting the principal amorous episodes of कृष्ण and राधा. Though the tone of the poem is entirely secular often bordering on crude-ness, the style and diction are considered as agreeable.
There are reasons to believe that there were more Caṇḍīdāsas than one, with epithets such as Dīna, द्विज and Anantabaḍu. But it is difficult to come to any definite conclusions.

Caṇḍikāvrata
(‘vow associated with Caṇḍikā’)
------------------------------------------
It is a religious vow undertaken on the 8th and 9th days of each fortnight (both dark and bright) when the goddess Caṇḍikā is to be worshipped. ड़स्तिन्ग् is a necessary discipline. The vrata is spread over one year. It helps the worshipper to get मोथेर् Caṇḍikā’s grace and fulfil his desires.
